newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Bruton says party received cash from store chain.
newsitem.headline: Bruton says party received cash from store chain.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, caught up in a storm lashing the nation's political establishment, said on Thursday his Fine Gael party had received cash from a department store chain over a six-year period.

Bruton said Fine Gael, the major partner in the ruling coalition, had taken 180,000 punts ($298,000) from the Dunnes Stores group to cut the party's debt but had never accepted money in return for political favour or influence.
It followed opposition calls for publication of an accountants' report detailing payments by the high street giant.
Controversy over Dunnes' cash payments forced Transport Minister Michael Lowry to resign on Saturday.
Lowry admitted a newspaper report that the company had paid for the 200,000-punt renovation of his private home in 1993 when Fine Gael was in opposition but denied any impropriety.
Charles Haughey, prime minister for a decade until his 1992 resignation, was quoted by the Examiner newspaper on Thursday as denying that he was the recipient of a million-punt payment.

It said a source close to Haughey, a political giant of the opposition Fianna Fail party, "strongly denied" that he had received funds or had controlled any British bank account into which Dunnes Stores funds were paid. The newspaper said Haughey was seeking legal advice.
Bruton's statement was issued in the early hours of Thursday after days of speculation which has monopolised the airwaves, grabbed all major headlines and mesmerised the public.
On Wednesday the party had refused to reveal details of its funding on grounds of confidentiality, saying it was up to party benefactors to decide whether or not such payments should be made public.

Bruton's coalition ally, the Labour Party, said on Wednesday that it had received 15,000 punts from Dunnes Stores to help the succesful 1990 presidential election campaign of Mary Robinson, Ireland's first woman president.
Dunnes said on Wednesday it would make the accountants' report on its payments available to tax inspectors but would not publish it.
Government officials were expected to meet Dunnes' representatives on Thursday to try to get the report published.

The store chain commissioned the report from accountants Price Waterhouse after a boardroom split which led to the resignation of Ben Dunne, one of its founding partners. The company is a private family business. ($1=.6049 Punt)
